name: Making Better Tech Bets
subject: quantum-computing
subjectTitle: A Skeptic's Guide to Quantum Computing

lesson.title: Making Better Bets: The Course's Real Argument, All at Once
lesson.summary: The closing chapter draws the GPT framework, the hype cycle, bias compounding, base rate reasoning, and the seven required breakthroughs into one practical decision habit for betting on any technology, and closes by being honest that some bets, evaluated this way, are genuinely worth taking.
lesson.body:
Everything in this course has been aimed at a single, practical capability, and it is worth naming plainly now that all the pieces are on the table: deciding, with calibrated confidence rather than borrowed enthusiasm or reflexive doubt, whether a hyped technology is actually worth betting time, money, or a career on. Quantum computing was the training ground, chosen because it is real, ongoing, and documented well enough to practice on, but the method was never really about qubits. This chapter is where that method gets stated as one thing instead of many separate lessons.

Start with the question that should come first, before any bet size gets discussed: is this even a General Purpose Technology candidate, and if so, which of its claimed breakthroughs are engineering problems and which are open scientific questions. The GPT framework's three tests, broad applicability across sectors, sustained improvement over time, and enabling a wave of complementary innovation, tell you whether a technology could plausibly earn the scale of excitement being asked of you at all. Each breakthrough is uncertain then tells you how to read the fine print of that promise honestly, separating the qubit count and error rate work that has a track record of yielding to sustained investment from the algorithmic and coherence questions that might not resolve on any schedule money can buy. A technology can pass the GPT tests in principle and still be a bad bet today, if the specific breakthroughs standing between now and that future sit mostly on the deep uncertainty side of that line.

Next comes the question of where you are on the curve, and here the hype cycle earns its keep as a practical timing tool rather than as background trivia. A Peak of Inflated Expectations and a Trough of Disillusionment are not signs that a technology is fake, plenty of genuine General Purpose Technologies, electricity and the internet among them, passed through both on their way to a real Plateau of Productivity. What the hype cycle actually tells you is that public enthusiasm and underlying technical readiness are different variables that move on different timelines, and that the loudest moment for a technology's coverage is rarely the moment its risk-adjusted return is most attractive. Knowing which phase a claim is riding does not tell you whether the technology is real. It tells you how much of the current price, attention, or urgency is coming from sentiment rather than from resolved technical uncertainty.

None of this analysis happens from a neutral vantage point, which is why the bias and incentive work sits underneath everything else rather than beside it. How biases compound showed that anchoring, sunk cost, bandwagon effects, and optimism bias reinforce each other inside real organizations, turning a series of small, individually reasonable choices into one large, hard to reverse collective bet. Base rate reasoning and the extraordinary claims rule showed how much evidence a given claim actually needs before it earns belief, scaled to how much it would overturn if true. Skipping either check does not just risk missing a red flag, it risks systematically mispricing the bet in the direction your own incentives and social environment are already pulling you.

Put the pieces together and a workable process falls out, the same one the skeptical inquiry method built in the previous chapter, now aimed specifically at a bet rather than a single claim. Ask what kind of technology this actually is against the GPT tests. Sort its remaining obstacles into engineering uncertainty and deep uncertainty rather than treating them as one undifferentiated pile of hard problems. Locate where public enthusiasm currently sits on the hype cycle and ask honestly whether that has drifted away from the technical evidence in either direction. Name the biases this particular bet is likely to activate in you or your organization before they compound into something harder to walk back. And size the bet the way the portfolio allocation chapters taught, treating a technology weighted toward deep uncertainty as a genuine, correlated risk, not diversified away just because it has a different logo attached, and small enough that walking away later, if the evidence turns, is still a live option rather than a sunk cost trap.

It would be a betrayal of everything this course has actually argued to end by telling you to distrust every exciting technology claim you encounter from here on. That is not what skepticism, done honestly, produces. The steam engine, electricity, and the transistor all cleared the GPT tests, all survived their own trough of disillusionment, and all rewarded the investors, engineers, and institutions patient and careful enough to keep backing them through the parts of the curve that looked, at the time, indistinguishable from every failed hype cycle around them. The entire point of building a method instead of a mood is that it lets you tell those two situations apart, not perfectly, nothing does, but far better than either uncritical enthusiasm or blanket cynicism ever could. You now have a real technical understanding of what quantum computing is and is not, a framework for judging any technology that depends on several uncertain breakthroughs landing together, and a transferable habit for pricing excitement against evidence that travels to whatever the next hyped technology turns out to be. Use it to say no more often than hype alone would have let you. Use it, just as importantly, to say yes, with real confidence, when the evidence actually earns it.
